title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: U-M's Textile Road choice highlights power, tax and local resistance issues statewide.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's just after 7 on this Thursday evening, and the University of Michigan has named Textile Road its preferred spot for a new data center project.
That choice lands right in Washtenaw County, but the ripple effects on power demand and taxes could reach listeners 30 miles away or more.
Exactly. Tonight we're digging into what this means for electric bills, water use, farmland and local services, plus the growing pushback we're seeing across the state.
Graham, walk us through the basics of this U-M announcement first.
The university picked the Textile Road location as its top choice for the project. It would add significant power demand in the area and could bring tax revenue, but only if it moves forward.
Why does picking one site matter so much beyond the immediate neighbors?
Because data centers pull huge amounts of electricity and water. Regulators and utilities are already talking about how to handle billions in new costs, and those get passed along through rates.
So this isn't just a Washtenaw story. How does it connect to the bigger picture of data center growth here?
Michigan is seeing proposals pop up in multiple counties, from northern areas to suburbs near Detroit. Each one raises the same questions about who pays for the infrastructure.
What kind of history are we looking at with these projects?

Over the past couple years we've had everything from crypto facilities to AI-focused ones. Some got built and now residents are dealing with noise complaints, while others are still in the planning stage facing local rules.
Who are the main players in this Textile Road decision?
U-M is driving it, but local township officials, utility companies like DTE, and nearby residents all have a stake. The county would feel the service demands if it advances.
And what about the tax side? I saw something about exemptions being challenged elsewhere.

Yes, a similar deal in Saline Township for an Oracle campus is facing a legal challenge from an attorney. It would skip years of property taxes on a multibillion-dollar project, shifting that burden to other Washtenaw County taxpayers.
How does that lost revenue actually hit regular people?

Townships and counties rely on property taxes for roads, schools and emergency services. When a big project gets a break, everyone else makes up the difference through higher bills or reduced services.
Power is another big piece. What's happening with the utilities?

DTE and Consumers Energy are pushing regulators to keep automatic rate hikes in place because data centers are driving up demand. Michigan regulators want lawmakers to change how those companies earn money so costs aren't automatically passed on.
If those changes don't happen, what does it mean for monthly bills?
Ratepayers across the state could see increases tied to the new infrastructure needed for these large users. Even folks far from any substation feel it when the overall system has to expand.
There's also talk of a court fight over a DTE data-center contract. How does that fit?

A legal challenge to one AI data-center power deal is questioning DTE's biggest new revenue source. If it unravels, plans to serve massive loads in southeast Michigan could face delays, and ratepayers might end up covering any shortfalls.
What happens next on the U-M project specifically?
Local reviews and possible public input will come next. The choice is preferred, but it still has to clear zoning, environmental checks and utility agreements.
Are other communities already putting rules in place to handle this?

Yes. Iosco County leaders are reviewing a draft ordinance that would limit size, noise and power use for future data centers. Chippewa County approved a full 12-month moratorium yesterday to study the impacts first.
That moratorium sounds like a pause button. Why are rural counties especially concerned?
Cheap land and available power attract big tech, but small townships worry about straining their grids and water supplies without enough tax base to cover it.
We've also seen pushback closer to Detroit. What's going on in those townships?

A Detroit-area township is trying to block or shrink a proposed project over noise, traffic and grid strain. In Richmond Township, hundreds of residents showed up yesterday to question impacts on roads, water and their own power bills.
Tax breaks seem to be a flashpoint everywhere.
Officials in Richmond heard direct complaints about giving breaks to the project while residents worry about higher costs. It's the same tension we see in the Saline challenge.
Noise has been an issue in at least one place already. What happened in Dowagiac?

Yesterday residents there sued over nonstop high-pitched noise from a crypto data center that's been running for two years. The company was fined and plans fixes, but neighbors want real soundproofing or buyouts.
How does all this affect farmland and water specifically?
Large facilities can take prime agricultural land out of production and pull millions of gallons of water daily for cooling. Townships are starting to write rules to protect those resources.
Regulators mentioned yesterday that new policies could actually lower rates even with more demand. How?
They told lawmakers that better planning and oversight of big users might keep overall costs down. It depends on what the legislature does with power planning rules.
So the U-M site choice is really a test case for how the state handles the next wave.
It is. If it advances, it sets a precedent for how power gets allocated and who pays. If it stalls, it shows local concerns can slow things down.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
More public meetings, possible legal filings on tax deals, and utility filings at the state level. The map on our tracker will update as new details drop.
Thanks for laying that out. This feels like the start of a much longer conversation across Michigan.
It does. Now let's move to some quick hits on the other stories from today and yesterday.
First, the Oracle tax exemption challenge in Saline Township. An attorney is fighting the abatement that would let the company skip years of taxes on a multibillion-dollar campus.
Washtenaw County taxpayers would cover the lost revenue while the project still draws heavy power and water. The hearing process is just getting started.
Next, DTE and Consumers are pushing to keep their automatic rate hikes as data centers increase demand.
Regulators want lawmakers to scrap those hikes and change how the utilities make money so the billions in new costs aren't automatically passed to residents.
A separate court fight over a DTE AI data-center contract is raising questions about the utility's growth plans.
If that deal unravels, southeast Michigan projects could see delays, and ratepayers might absorb any extra costs for backup power.
In Iosco County, leaders are drafting rules to limit data center size, noise and power use.
East Tawas area residents could see those standards in place soon as big tech looks north for cheap land.
A Detroit-area township is actively fighting a proposed data center over noise, traffic and grid strain.
Even smaller projects are now drawing organized local resistance, which could become a pattern.
Yesterday in Richmond Township, hundreds of residents grilled backers on roads, water and power bills.
Officials heard complaints about noise and tax breaks, signaling growing pushback in Macomb County.
Also yesterday, Dowagiac neighbors sued over nonstop noise from a crypto data center that's been an issue for two years.
The company faces demands for real soundproofing after already getting fined under new local limits.
State regulators told lawmakers yesterday that new policies could lower electricity rates even with data center growth.
The outcome depends on what the legislature does on power planning.
And Chippewa County approved a 12-month moratorium on new data center proposals yesterday.
That gives the rural Upper Peninsula county time to study power, water and zoning impacts before anything moves forward.
Now for what's on deck. Tonight there are a couple of key meetings listeners can attend or follow.
The Negaunee City Council or Planning Commission has a public hearing on a proposed data center ordinance that would limit facilities to mining and industrial zones with noise and height standards.
Also tonight, the Michigan for Responsible Data Centers Coalition is holding a virtual town hall on Van Buren Township construction and regulations.
Then on Monday the 17th, the Kalamazoo City Commission will vote on a resolution for a temporary moratorium on data center development.
Plenty for folks to weigh in on if these issues hit close to home.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening, everyone. Good night.

episode_title: U-M Picks Textile Road Site, Igniting Broader Fight Over Data Center Costs and Impacts
